concept.name: Mutation Testing

relationships.description: Connects Mutation Testing to contract testing in the broader engineering catalog.

spark.summary: Mutation testing evaluates the quality of your test suite by automatically injecting tiny bugs ('mutants')—like flipping `>` to `>=` or removing a return value—into production code and checking whether your tests fail. A mutant that survives exposes a blind spot where 100% line coverage gave false confidence.
spark.keyTakeaway: Code coverage measures which lines your tests executed; mutation testing measures whether your assertions actually catch bugs on those lines.

concept.whyItMatters: A test suite can hit 95% line coverage while having weak or missing assertions—executing a discount calculation without ever asserting the final price. Mutation testing (using tools like PITest for Java, Stryker for TypeScript/C#, or `mutmut` for Python) surfaces these 'assertion-free' tests quantitatively via the Mutation Score, catching subtle off-by-one, boundary, and null-handling bugs before production.
whenToUse: High-risk business logic: pricing engines, tax/interest calculators, authorization policies, state machines, and protocol parsers.
Legacy or AI-generated codebases where high line coverage masks weak, tautological, or missing assertions.
Scoped PR diffs (`--since main` / incremental mode) in CI to verify new logic is genuinely tested without running on the whole repo.
whenNotToUse: Running full-repository mutation suites on every commit in a 500K-line monolith—executing tests per mutant causes 10x–50x CI runtime blowups.
Thin CRUD glue, DTOs, generated protobuf/OpenAPI bindings, or UI layout code where mutants mostly produce noise or equivalent code.
Projects with slow, flaky integration tests (e.g., spinning up Docker/Selenium per test) where a 10-minute baseline suite turns into an 8-hour mutation run.
keyPoints: Each mutant is a single syntactic change (e.g., `+` -> `-`, `true` -> `false`, `a && b` -> `a || b`) applied to compiled bytecode or the AST.
Mutant outcomes fall into four buckets: Killed (test failed—good), Survived (tests passed—gap!), Timed Out (infinite loop—usually counted as killed), and No Coverage.
Mutation Score = `Killed / (Total - Equivalent)` (or `Killed / Covered`); aim for 80–90% on critical modules rather than chasing 100%.
Equivalent mutants (e.g., changing `i < 10` to `i != 10` in a `+1` loop) have identical observable behavior and can never be killed—don't waste hours trying.
Fast feedback depends on scoping: use git-diff filtering, coverage-guided test selection (running only tests that touch the mutated line), and parallel workers.

examples.title: Catching a Boundary Bug in Tiered Pricing (Java / PITest)
examples.scenario: A billing service has 100% branch coverage on `if (units > 100) applyBulkDiscount()`. PITest mutates `>` to `>=` (Conditionals Boundary Mutator). All unit tests still pass because tests only checked `units = 50` and `units = 150`.
examples.outcome: The surviving mutant flags the missing `units == 100` boundary test; adding a single assertion kills the mutant and prevents an off-by-one overcharge.

examples.title: Incremental PR Gate in TypeScript (Stryker)
examples.scenario: A fintech team configures Stryker with `--incremental` and git-diff scoping in GitHub Actions on their `src/ledger/` directory, capping execution to 4 minutes.
examples.outcome: PRs modifying ledger rules must maintain >=85% mutation score on changed lines, catching missing negative-balance and idempotency assertions automatically.

tradeOffs.factor: Execution Scope (Full Repo vs. PR Diff / Critical Modules)
tradeOffs.pro: Diff-scoped incremental mutation runs in 1–4 minutes per PR while protecting all new business logic.
tradeOffs.con: Leaves untouched legacy modules unmeasured unless paired with a scheduled nightly full run.

tradeOffs.pro: Default mutator sets (conditionals, math, return values, void method calls) yield high signal with minimal equivalent-mutant noise.
tradeOffs.con: Enabling every string/constant mutator generates thousands of low-value survivors (e.g., log message edits).

tradeOffs.pro: Enforcing a hard 80–85% threshold on critical packages prevents test quality regression.
tradeOffs.con: Setting a rigid 95%+ gate forces engineers to write brittle tests against equivalent mutants or log strings.

failureModes.name: CI Timeout Explosion
failureModes.description: A team enables PITest or Stryker across an entire 100K-line service without coverage filtering, spawning 15,000 mutants against a 3-minute test suite.
failureModes.mitigation: Enable coverage-based test filtering (run only tests covering the mutated line), restrict to critical packages, and run full sweeps nightly.

failureModes.name: Equivalent Mutant Fatigue
failureModes.description: Engineers burn hours trying to kill a mutant that is semantically identical to the original code (e.g., mutating a performance-only cache check or loop condition).
failureModes.mitigation: Accept an 80–90% target ceiling, configure mutator exclusions for logging/metrics, and use inline suppression annotations sparingly.

failureModes.name: Flaky Test False Kills
failureModes.description: A timing-dependent or network-flaky unit test fails randomly during a mutant run, falsely marking a weak mutant as 'Killed'.
failureModes.mitigation: Quarantine flaky tests, enforce deterministic clocks/mocks in unit tests, and run mutation testing only on isolated unit suites.

failureModes.name: Infinite Loop Mutant Hang
failureModes.description: Mutating a loop increment or exit condition creates an infinite loop that hangs the test worker.
failureModes.mitigation: Rely on the tool's per-mutant timeout multiplier (typically `1.5x * baseline_test_time + 500ms`) so hung workers are terminated cleanly.

commonMistakes: Targeting 100% mutation score across the whole codebase instead of focusing on core domain logic.
Running mutation testing on slow end-to-end or database-backed tests instead of fast in-memory unit tests.
Forgetting to exclude logging, `toString()`, and telemetry statements, flooding reports with useless surviving mutants.
Interpreting 'No Coverage' mutants as a mutation-testing problem when basic line coverage isn't even established yet.
Running without `--incremental` or SCM diff filtering in CI, causing developers to disable the check out of frustration.

sections.content:
## The idea

Traditional code coverage answers a weak question: *did a test execute line 42?* It cannot tell you whether the test would fail if line 42 were subtly wrong. **Mutation testing** flips the script by testing the tests themselves.

A mutation engine takes your compiled bytecode (like **PITest** for JVM) or AST (like **Stryker** for JS/TS/C# or **mutmut** for Python) and generates hundreds of slightly altered versions of your code called **mutants**—for example, changing `a > b` to `a >= b`, `&&` to `||`, or `return total` to `return 0`. It then runs your unit tests against each mutant. If at least one test fails, the mutant is **killed** (your tests caught the bug). If all tests pass, the mutant **survived**, exposing a concrete gap in your assertions.

## Concrete walkthrough

Consider a Java `ShippingCalculator` method with **100% line and branch coverage**:

```java
boolean qualifiesForFreeShipping(int cartTotalCents, boolean isVip) {
  return cartTotalCents >= 5000 || isVip;
}
```

1. **Baseline Run**: PITest runs the existing unit tests (`cartTotalCents = 6000, isVip = false` -> `true`; `cartTotalCents = 2000, isVip = false` -> `false`) and records which tests cover line 2 (total time: 180ms).
2. **Mutant Generation**: PITest applies mutators to bytecode:
   - **M1 (Boundary)**: `>= 5000` -> `> 5000`
   - **M2 (Boolean)**: `||` -> `&&`
   - **M3 (Return)**: `return false`
3. **Targeted Execution**: Only the 2 tests covering line 2 execute against M1, M2, and M3.
4. **Results**: M2 and M3 fail the `6000, false` test (**Killed**). M1 (`> 5000`) passes both tests (**Survived**!) because no test checked `cartTotalCents == 5000`.
5. **Fix**: Adding `assertTrue(qualifiesForFreeShipping(5000, false))` kills M1 and raises the module's Mutation Score from 66% to 100%.

data.title: Coverage-guided mutation testing pipeline

edges.label: Coverage map
edges.title: Collect baseline coverage
edges.description: Run the test suite once to verify green status and build a line-to-test coverage matrix.

edges.label: Single mutant
edges.title: Inject one fault per mutant
edges.description: Apply one operator (e.g., >= to >) on covered lines and skip uncovered or excluded code.

edges.label: Fast-fail subset
edges.title: Run only covering tests
edges.description: Execute only tests that touch the mutated line, stopping on the first failure or timeout.

edges.label: Classify outcome
edges.title: Record Killed or Survived
edges.description: Mark test failures/timeouts as Killed and passing runs as Survived gaps.

edges.label: Add assertions
edges.title: Close assertion gaps
edges.description: Developers inspect surviving mutants to add boundary or state assertions and re-verify.

data.caption: Coverage-guided filtering and fail-fast execution keep mutation testing fast enough for pull-request CI gates.

sections.content:
## Mutator operators and speed optimizations

Modern mutation engines avoid recompiling for every mutant. **PITest** mutates JVM bytecode directly in memory; **Stryker** uses mutant switching (embedding all mutants behind a runtime `activeMutant` environment switch in one compile pass). Combined with **fail-fast** execution (aborting remaining tests the instant one test kills the mutant) and **git-diff scoping**, runtime drops by 10x–30x.

Core operator families include **Conditionals Boundary** (`<` -> `<=`), **Negate Conditionals** (`==` -> `!=`), **Math** (`+` -> `-`), **Return Values** (`true` -> `false`, `list` -> `emptyList()`), and **Void Method Calls** (deleting side-effecting calls like `auditLog.record()`).

## Ecosystem tooling comparison

| Tool | Language / Runtime | Mutation Mechanism | Key Speed Feature | Typical Best Fit |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **PITest** | Java / Kotlin (JVM) | In-memory bytecode manipulation | Coverage-guided + incremental history | Spring Boot services, financial/domain jars |
| **Stryker** | JS / TS / C# / Scala | AST + mutant switching | `--incremental` + git diff + parallel workers | TypeScript backends, React logic, .NET APIs |
| **mutmut** | Python | AST transformation | Incremental cache + pytest `-x` fail-fast | Python data pipelines, FastAPI business rules |
| **cargo-mutants** | Rust | Source-level AST edits | `--in-diff` PR filtering + cargo incremental | Rust parsers, crypto/consensus crates |

## Failure modes

The primary operational failure is **unbounded runtime** when teams run mutation testing on integration suites or un-scoped monoliths. A 5-minute test suite with 2,000 mutants can easily take 6+ hours if every mutant runs every test.

The second failure is **equivalent-mutant burnout**: when a mutant changes internal state without altering observable output (e.g., changing `capacity * 2` to `capacity + 1` in a dynamically resizing buffer), no unit test can kill it. Treating 100% mutation score as a hard CI requirement creates developer hostility and brittle tests.

## Practical CI/CD integration

Deploy mutation testing in two tiers:

1. **PR Gate (Fast, <4 min)**: Run only on files changed in the pull request (`--since main` / `--in-diff`), targeting core domain directories (`src/domain/`, `src/pricing/`). Enforce a realistic threshold (e.g., >=80% on covered mutants).
2. **Nightly Deep Sweep**: Run across all critical packages, publish HTML reports to CI artifacts, and track Mutation Score trends over time alongside traditional line coverage.

## Practical checklist

- [ ] **Target critical modules first**: Start with pricing, auth, validation, and state-machine packages—skip DTOs and boilerplate.
- [ ] **Isolate fast unit tests**: Ensure baseline unit tests run in <10 seconds with zero network or DB dependencies.
- [ ] **Exclude noisy code**: Filter out loggers, metrics, `equals/hashCode`, and generated files from mutation.
- [ ] **Enable incremental/diff mode**: Configure `--incremental` or SCM diff filtering before enabling PR checks.
- [ ] **Set realistic thresholds**: Target 80–90% Mutation Score to account for equivalent mutants without blocking velocity.

interviewProblems.title: Mutation Testing
interviewProblems.scenarioPrompt: Design a production system that depends on Mutation Testing. What invariants, failure modes, and observability do you require?
interviewProblems.sampleDefense: Start from invariants, choose the pattern that preserves them, and add metrics for the known failure modes.
commonPitfalls: Optimizing throughput before defining correctness boundaries.

steps.title: 1. Normal Request Ingress
steps.explanation: Mutation testing evaluates the quality of your test suite by automatically injecting tiny bugs ('mutants')—like flipping `>` to `>=` or removing a return value—into production code and checking whether your tests fail. A mutant that survives exposes a blind spot where 100% line coverage gave false confidence.

steps.title: 2. Core Execution & State Lookup
steps.explanation: Sandboxed Test Runner applies the primary invariant and coordinates with Mutation Report.

steps.title: 3. Scale Spike / Failure Injection
steps.explanation: Under a 10x burst, Mutation Report experiences contention and tail-latency amplification.

steps.title: 4. Mitigation & Steady Recovery
steps.explanation: Enable coverage-based test filtering (run only tests covering the mutated line), restrict to critical packages, and run full sweeps nightly.

tipsAndTricks: Core mental model: Code coverage measures which lines your tests executed; mutation testing measures whether your assertions actually catch bugs on those lines.
Avoid trap: Targeting 100% mutation score across the whole codebase instead of focusing on core domain logic.
Avoid trap: Running mutation testing on slow end-to-end or database-backed tests instead of fast in-memory unit tests.
When to reach for it: High-risk business logic: pricing engines, tax/interest calculators, authorization policies, state machines, and protocol parsers.
When to reach for it: Legacy or AI-generated codebases where high line coverage masks weak, tautological, or missing assertions.

putItTogether.title: Putting Mutation Testing Together
putItTogether.summary: Code coverage measures which lines your tests executed; mutation testing measures whether your assertions actually catch bugs on those lines.
steps: Establish baseline invariants for Mutation Testing before scaling.
Isolate hot paths with caching, backpressure, or partitioning.
Verify failure modes with synthetic load & chaos checks.
putItTogether.outcome: The surviving mutant flags the missing `units == 100` boundary test; adding a single assertion kills the mutant and prevents an off-by-one overcharge.
